lehigh-2026-01.title: Middle term is the average
lehigh-2026-01.body:
In an arithmetic sequence of $5$ terms the middle term $a_2$ equals the average of all terms: $30/5=6$. (The terms are $6-2d,6-d,6,6+d,6+2d$.)

**Answer: 6**

lehigh-2026-05.title: Count factors of 5
lehigh-2026-05.body:
Trailing zeros come from pairs of factors $2$ and $5$; there are far more $2$'s, so count the $5$'s: $\lfloor\tfrac{2026}5\rfloor+\lfloor\tfrac{2026}{25}\rfloor+\lfloor\tfrac{2026}{125}\rfloor+\lfloor\tfrac{2026}{625}\rfloor=405+81+16+3=505$.

**Answer: 505**

lehigh-2026-06.title: Difference of squares
lehigh-2026-06.body:
Let $n+p=b^2$ and $n+7p=a^2$ with $a,b\ge0$. Then $6p=a^2-b^2=(a+b)(a-b)$. The two factors have the same parity and their product is even, so both are even and the product is divisible by $4$. Thus $4\mid6p$, so $p$ is even: $p=2$.

It works: $n=2$ gives $n+p=4$ and $n+7p=16$.

**Answer: $p=2$**

lehigh-2026-07.title: Vieta
lehigh-2026-07.body:
If the roots are $r,s,t$: $\dfrac1r+\dfrac1s+\dfrac1t=\dfrac{rs+rt+st}{rst}=\dfrac{13}{7}$ (sum of pairwise products $13$, product of roots $7$).

**Answer: $13/7$**

lehigh-2026-09.title: Solve $LW=2(L+W)$
lehigh-2026-09.body:
$LW=2L+2W$ gives $(L-2)(W-2)=4$. With $L\ge W\ge1$, $W-2\ge-1$: the factor pairs are $(L-2,W-2)=(4,1),(2,2)$ (and $(-1,-4)$ etc. give nonpositive sides). So $(L,W)=(6,3)$ and $(4,4)$.

Areas: $18$ and $16$. Sum $=34$.

**Answer: 34**

lehigh-2026-10.title: Coordinates
lehigh-2026-10.body:
Put $A=(0,0)$, $B=(1,0)$, $C=(0,\tfrac43)$, $D=(0,1)$. Then $BD$ has length $\sqrt2$, and $E$ is on $BD$ at distance $1$ from $B$: $E=\left(1-\tfrac1{\sqrt2},\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\right)$. So $F=\left(0,\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\right)$ and $G=\left(1,\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\right)$.

The flag is the region bounded by $AB$, $BE$, $EG$, $GC$, $CA$: the quadrilateral $ABEF$ together with triangle $CFG$.

$ABEF$ is a trapezoid with parallel sides $AB=1$ and $FE=1-\tfrac1{\sqrt2}$, height $\tfrac1{\sqrt2}$: area $\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\cdot\tfrac12\left(2-\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\right)=\tfrac1{\sqrt2}-\tfrac14$.

$CFG$ has base $FG=1$ and height $CF=\tfrac43-\tfrac1{\sqrt2}$: area $\tfrac23-\tfrac1{2\sqrt2}$.

Total $=\tfrac23-\tfrac14+\tfrac1{\sqrt2}-\tfrac1{2\sqrt2}=\tfrac5{12}+\tfrac1{2\sqrt2}=\tfrac5{12}+\tfrac{\sqrt2}4=\dfrac{5+3\sqrt2}{12}$.

**Answer: $\dfrac{5+3\sqrt2}{12}$**

lehigh-2026-11.title: Chinese Remainder Theorem
lehigh-2026-11.body:
Let $x$ be the number of candies: $x\equiv5\pmod{21}$ and $x\equiv3\pmod{22}$. Since $\gcd(21,22)=1$ the solution is unique mod $462$.

Write $x=22m+3$; then $22m+3\equiv m+3\equiv5\pmod{21}$, so $m\equiv2\pmod{21}$, $x=22(2+21t)+3=47+462t$.

The smallest such value above $400$ is $47+462=509$.

**Answer: 509**

lehigh-2026-12.title: Bayes
lehigh-2026-12.body:
Each of the $4$ choices of (die, die) has probability $\tfrac14$: same die with probability $\tfrac12$, different dice with probability $\tfrac12$.

Same die (either): sums of $9$: $(3,6),(4,5),(5,4),(6,3)$ for die 1, and the same four for die 2, so $\tfrac4{36}$. Different dice: $(1,8),(2,7),(3,6),(4,5),(5,4),(6,3)$, so $\tfrac6{36}$.

$P(\text{same and }9)=\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac4{36}=\tfrac1{18}$, $P(\text{different and }9)=\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac6{36}=\tfrac1{12}$.

Conditional probability $=\dfrac{1/18}{1/18+1/12}=\dfrac{2/36}{2/36+3/36}=\dfrac25$.

**Answer: $2/5$**

lehigh-2026-14.title: Count and divide by 6
lehigh-2026-14.body:
Count positive triples with sum $100$ in any order: $\binom{99}2=4851=99\cdot49$. Those with two equal entries: choose the repeated value $k$ with $2k<100$ ($k=1,\dots,49$) and the position of the odd one ($3$ ways), but $k=100/3$ is impossible so there is no triple with all equal: $3\cdot49=147$.

Triples with all distinct entries: $4851-147=4704$, each set counted $6$ times. So $4704/6=784$ triples with $a>b>c$.

**Answer: 784**

lehigh-2026-15.title: Subtract areas
lehigh-2026-15.body:
Since $X$ lies on $DP$, $[PQX]=[PQD]-[QDX]$. Triangle $PQD$ has base $DQ=1$ on $DC$ and height $PC=3$, so $[PQD]=\tfrac32$.

Let $\theta=\angle CDP$. Then $\tan\theta=\tfrac{PC}{DC}=\tfrac34$, so $\sin\theta=\tfrac35$, $\cos\theta=\tfrac45$. The angle $QDX$ equals $\theta$ (as $Q$ is on $DC$), and $\angle XDA=90^\circ-\theta$.

Let $t=DX$. Triangle $QDA$ has area $\tfrac12\cdot DQ\cdot DA=2$ and is split by $DX$:
$$2=[QDX]+[XDA]=\tfrac12\cdot1\cdot t\sin\theta+\tfrac12\cdot4\cdot t\cos\theta=\tfrac3{10}t+\tfrac85t=\tfrac{19}{10}t.$$
So $t=\tfrac{20}{19}$ and $[QDX]=\tfrac3{10}\cdot\tfrac{20}{19}=\tfrac6{19}$.

$[PQX]=\tfrac32-\tfrac6{19}=\dfrac{45}{38}$.

**Answer: $45/38$**

lehigh-2026-15.title: Coordinates
lehigh-2026-15.body: Take $A=(0,0)$, $B=(4,0)$, $C=(4,4)$, $D=(0,4)$, so $P=(4,1)$, $Q=(1,4)$. Line $AQ$: $y=4x$; line $DP$: $y=4-\tfrac34x$. They meet at $x=\tfrac{16}{19}$, $X=\left(\tfrac{16}{19},\tfrac{64}{19}\right)$. The shoelace formula for $P,Q,X$ gives area $\tfrac{45}{38}$.

lehigh-2026-16.title: Triangle inequality
lehigh-2026-16.body:
$x^2+4x+8=(x+2)^2+2^2$ and $x^2+2x+10=(x+1)^2+3^2$. With $P=(x,0)$, $A=(-2,2)$, $B=(-1,3)$ the expression is $|PA-PB|$.

By the triangle inequality $|PA-PB|\le AB=\sqrt2$, with equality exactly when $P$ lies on line $AB$ outside the segment. Line $AB$ is $y=x+4$, meeting the $x$-axis at $P=(-4,0)$ (outside segment $AB$). So the maximum $\sqrt2$ occurs at $x=-4$.

**Answer: $-4$**

lehigh-2026-17.title: Linearity of expectation
lehigh-2026-17.body:
For each color, the probability that it is drawn at least once in four draws is $1-\left(\tfrac9{10}\right)^4=1-\tfrac{6561}{10000}=\tfrac{3439}{10000}$. By linearity, the expected number of colors is $10\cdot\tfrac{3439}{10000}=\tfrac{3439}{1000}=3.439$.

**Answer: $3.439$**

lehigh-2026-18.title: Cut off three similar triangles
lehigh-2026-18.body:
Heron: $s=10$, $[ABC]=\sqrt{10\cdot5\cdot2\cdot3}=10\sqrt3$. The inradius is $r=\tfrac{[ABC]}s=\sqrt3$.

The line $DE\parallel BC$ tangent to the incircle cuts off a triangle $ADE$ similar to $ABC$. The altitude from $A$ to $BC$ is $h_A=\tfrac{2[ABC]}7=\tfrac{20\sqrt3}7$, and the tangent line is at distance $2r$ closer to $A$ than $BC$ (incircle diameter), so the altitude of $ADE$ is $h_A-2r=\tfrac{6\sqrt3}7$; the ratio is $\tfrac{6}{20}=\tfrac3{10}$ and $[ADE]=\tfrac9{100}[ABC]$.

Similarly $h_B=\tfrac{2[ABC]}{AC}=\tfrac{5\sqrt3}2$, altitude of $BHJ$: $\tfrac{5\sqrt3}2-2\sqrt3=\tfrac{\sqrt3}2$, ratio $\tfrac15$, area $\tfrac1{25}[ABC]$. And $h_C=\tfrac{2[ABC]}{AB}=4\sqrt3$, altitude of $CFG$: $2\sqrt3$, ratio $\tfrac12$, area $\tfrac14[ABC]$.

Hexagon area $=[ABC]\left(1-\tfrac9{100}-\tfrac1{25}-\tfrac14\right)=10\sqrt3\cdot\tfrac{62}{100}=\dfrac{31\sqrt3}5$.

**Answer: $\dfrac{31\sqrt3}{5}$**

lehigh-2026-19.title: Weighted AM-GM
lehigh-2026-19.body:
Split the expression into $11$ terms: two copies of $\tfrac{x^3}2$, three copies of $\tfrac{4y^2}3$ and six copies of $\tfrac{9z}6$ (these multiplicities make the powers of $x$, $y$, $z$ in the product equal). AM-GM gives
$$x^3+4y^2+9z\ge11\sqrt[11]{\left(\tfrac{x^3}2\right)^2\left(\tfrac{4y^2}3\right)^3\left(\tfrac{9z}6\right)^6}=11\sqrt[11]{(xyz)^6\cdot\tfrac14\cdot\tfrac{64}{27}\cdot\tfrac{729}{64}}=11\sqrt[11]{\tfrac{27}4}.$$
Equality needs all $11$ terms equal, $\tfrac{x^3}2=\tfrac{4y^2}3=\tfrac{9z}6$, which together with $xyz=1$ has a solution, so the bound is attained.

**Answer: $11\sqrt[11]{27/4}\approx13.085$**

lehigh-2026-19.title: Numerical check
lehigh-2026-19.body: Minimizing $x^3+4y^2+\tfrac9{xy}$ over a fine grid gives about $13.085$, matching $11(27/4)^{1/11}$.

lehigh-2026-20.title: Forced moves
lehigh-2026-20.body:
Call a diagonal step $(1,1)$ a $D$ (it raises $m+n$ by $2$) and a horizontal or vertical step an $S$ (raises $m+n$ by $1$). Look at $m+n\bmod3$. At a point with $m+n\equiv1$: a $D$ would land on $\equiv0$ (forbidden), so an $S$ is forced (to $\equiv2$). At $m+n\equiv2$: an $S$ would land on $\equiv0$, so a $D$ is forced (to $\equiv1$).

From $(0,0)$ we may start with $D$ or $S$.

- Start with $D$ ($m+n=2$): then the moves are forced, giving $D\,(DS)^8\,D$ (total $m+n$: $2+24+2=28$). It has $8$ $S$'s, and exactly $4$ must be horizontal and $4$ vertical: $\binom84=70$ paths.
- Start with $S$ ($m+n=1$): forced $S$, then $D,S,D,S,\dots$: $SS\,(DS)^8\,D$, with $10$ $S$'s, $5$ horizontal and $5$ vertical: $\binom{10}5=252$ paths.

Total $70+252=322$.

**Answer: 322**

lehigh-2026-20.title: Dynamic programming
lehigh-2026-20.body: Fill a table of path counts, with $0$ at every point with $m+n\equiv0\pmod 3$ other than $(0,0)$, and elsewhere the sum of the counts at $(m-1,n)$, $(m,n-1)$, $(m-1,n-1)$. The entry at $(14,14)$ is $322$.

lehigh-2026-21.title: Translate to the origin
lehigh-2026-21.body:
Write $z_1=w_1$, $z_2=4-2i+w_2$, $z_3=2+8i+w_3$ with $|w_1|=1$, $|w_2|=2$, $|w_3|=4$. The sum is $6+6i+(w_1+w_2+w_3)$, so we need the area of the set $S$ of all values $w_1+w_2+w_3$.

$S$ is unchanged by rotating about $0$ (rotate all three vectors together). For the modulus: $|w_1+w_2+w_3|\le1+2+4=7$ and $|w_1+w_2+w_3|\ge|w_3|-|w_2|-|w_1|=1$. Both extremes occur ($w_1=w_2=w_3=1$ gives $7$; $w_3=4$, $w_2=-2$, $w_1=-1$ gives $1$), and as the angles vary continuously the modulus takes every value in $[1,7]$.

Hence $S$ is the annulus $1\le|w|\le7$, with area $\pi(7^2-1^2)=48\pi$.

**Answer: $48\pi$**

lehigh-2026-22.title: Golden ratio lengths
lehigh-2026-22.body:
Let the big pentagon have side $s$ and diagonal $d=\varphi s$, where $\varphi=\tfrac{1+\sqrt5}2$ (so $\varphi^2=\varphi+1$, $\varphi-1=\tfrac1\varphi$).

Take the diagonal $AC$ of pentagon $ABCDE$. The diagonals $BE$ and $BD$ cross it at $X$ and $Y$. Triangle $ABX$ has base angles $36^\circ$, so $AX=\dfrac{s/2}{\cos36^\circ}=\dfrac s\varphi$ (as $2\cos36^\circ=\varphi$); by symmetry $CY=\dfrac s\varphi$. The middle piece $XY$ is a side of the inner pentagon:
$$x=XY=\varphi s-\frac{2s}\varphi=s\cdot\frac{\varphi^2-2}{\varphi}=s\cdot\frac{\varphi-1}{\varphi}=\frac s{\varphi^2}.$$
So the side ratio is $\dfrac1{\varphi^2}=\dfrac{3-\sqrt5}2$ and the area ratio is its square:
$$\left(\frac{3-\sqrt5}2\right)^2=\frac{14-6\sqrt5}4=\frac{7-3\sqrt5}2\approx0.146.$$

**Answer: $\dfrac{7-3\sqrt5}{2}$**

lehigh-2026-22.title: Numerical check
lehigh-2026-22.body: Placing the vertices at the fifth roots of unity and intersecting the diagonals numerically gives an inner pentagon of area ratio $0.1459\ldots=\tfrac{7-3\sqrt5}2$.

lehigh-2026-23.title: Count factorizations
lehigh-2026-23.body:
Write $n=a^2-b^2=uv$ with $u=a-b\le v=a+b$. Conversely $u,v$ give integers $a=\tfrac{u+v}2$, $b=\tfrac{v-u}2\ge0$ exactly when $u\le v$ have the same parity. So the number of ways is the number of unordered factorizations $n=uv$ with $u,v$ of the same parity.

- $n\equiv2\pmod4$: no ways.
- $n$ odd: all divisors are odd, so the number of ways is $\lceil d(n)/2\rceil$.
- $4\mid n$: $u,v$ must both be even, $u=2u'$, $v=2v'$ with $u'v'=n/4$, so the number of ways is $\lceil d(n/4)/2\rceil$.

We need $\lceil d(m)/2\rceil=13$, i.e. $d(m)=25$ or $26$, where $m=n/4$ (or $m=n$ for odd $n$).

Smallest $m$ with $d(m)=25$: $2^4\cdot3^4=1296$ (other forms such as $2^{24}$, $2^2\cdot3^{4}\cdots$ are larger). Smallest $m$ with $d(m)=26$: $2^{12}\cdot3=12288$. So the best even case is $m=1296$, $n=4\cdot1296=5184$.

For odd $n$ the smallest number with $d=25$ using odd primes is $3^4\cdot5^4=50625$, which is bigger.

Hence the smallest such number is $5184=2^6\cdot3^4$.

**Answer: 5184**

lehigh-2026-23.title: Check by computer
lehigh-2026-23.body: Counting the representations $a^2-b^2=n$ for every $n<6000$ shows that $5184$ is the first $n$ with exactly $13$.

lehigh-2026-24.title: Where $01$ can appear
lehigh-2026-24.body:
$X_n$ is a concatenation of blocks, one per symbol of $X_{n-1}$: the block is $11000$ for a $1$ and $1$ for a $0$. Inside a block $11000$ there is no $01$. Every block starts with $1$, and a block ends with $0$ exactly when it is $11000$ (it came from a $1$). So a $01$ appears at each boundary that follows a $11000$ block, i.e. once for every $1$ of $X_{n-1}$ that is not the last symbol of $X_{n-1}$.

$X_{n-1}$ ends in $1$ when $n-1$ is odd ($X_1=1$; a final $1$ becomes $\dots0$, and a final $0$ becomes $1$). So with $v_n$ the number of $1$'s in $X_n$: $w_n=v_{n-1}$ for $n$ odd, $w_n=v_{n-1}-1$ for $n$ even.

**Counting the 1's.** With $u_n$ zeros: $u_{n+1}=3v_n$ and $v_{n+1}=2v_n+u_n=2v_n+3v_{n-1}$, $v_1=1$, $v_2=2$. The roots of $r^2-2r-3=0$ are $3$ and $-1$, so $v_n=\dfrac{3^n-(-1)^n}4$.

For $n=2026$ (even): $w_{2026}=v_{2025}-1=\dfrac{3^{2025}+1}4-1=\dfrac{3^{2025}-3}4$.

Check on small cases: $w_3=v_2=2$ (indeed $X_3=1100011000111$ has two $01$'s) and $w_4=v_3-1=6$.

**Answer: $\dfrac{3^{2025}-3}4$**

lehigh-2026-25.title: A better coordinate system
lehigh-2026-25.body:
Encode a pair $(x,y)$ as $[a,b]=[xy,\,x/y]$ (then $x=\sqrt{ab}$, $y=\sqrt{a/b}$). For the new pair $\left(\tfrac{xyx'}{y'},\tfrac{xyy'}{x'}\right)$ the product of entries is $(xy)^2$ and their ratio is $(x'/y')^2$. So merging $[a_1,b_1]$ and $[a_2,b_2]$ gives $[a_1^2,\,b_2^2]$: only the first entry of the left pair and the second entry of the right pair survive, each squared.

The leftmost original pair is $[2014,\tfrac{1007}2]$ and the rightmost is $[505\cdot504,\tfrac{505}{504}]$. If $\ell$ merges involve the block currently at the left end and $r$ merges involve the block currently at the right end, the final pair is
$$\left[2014^{2^{\ell}},\ \left(\tfrac{505}{504}\right)^{2^{r}}\right],$$
and different $(\ell,r)$ give different final pairs (both bases exceed $1$).

**Which $(\ell,r)$ occur?** Only the last merge involves both end blocks, so $\ell+r-1\le502$, i.e. $\ell+r\le503$; also $\ell,r\ge1$. The case $\ell=r=1$ is impossible (it would mean the final merge combines the two original end pairs, but $503>2$ pairs must all be absorbed). Every other $(\ell,r)$ with $\ell+r\le503$ can be realised: make $503-\ell-r$ merges in the middle, then $\ell-1$ merges on the left, then $r$ on the right.

Count: $\sum_{\ell=1}^{502}(503-\ell)-1=\dfrac{502\cdot503}2-1=126253-1=126252$.

**Answer: 126252**

lehigh-2026-25.title: Small cases
lehigh-2026-25.body: Enumerating all merge orders for $m=3,4,5,6,7$ pairs gives $2,5,9,14,20$ final pairs, matching $\tfrac{m(m-1)}2-1$; for $m=503$ this is $126252$.
